title: Tensions around Taiwan
subtitle: 23 million inhabitants, a dependent planet
subject: comprendreLeMonde
description: A 36,000 km² island manufactures most of the world's electronic chips. This is why **Taiwan** is one of the most dangerous places on the planet.

hero.hook: A small island makes the chips that power the world, and Beijing claims it as its province.

blocks.text: **Taiwan** is considered one of the most dangerous spots of the 21st century. For China, this island is only a rebel province which must one day “return” to the national fold. For its 23 million inhabitants, it is a sovereign democracy, born from a civil war that the rest of the world has almost forgotten.

Beyond questions of identity, Taiwan has become the beating heart of the global digital economy. This is what makes a possible armed conflict so frightening: it would threaten not just Asia, but every factory and smartphone on the planet.

sections.title: The legacy of 1949: the fracture of the two Chinas

blocks.text: It all starts from the **Chinese civil war**, which pitted the communists of Mao Zedong against the nationalists of the **[[Kuomintang]]**, led by Chiang Kai-shek. In 1949, crushed by the communist victory, the nationalists took refuge on the island of Taiwan, with the treasures of the Forbidden City and the structures of their state.

blocks.caption: In 1949, the Kuomintang nationalists retreated to the island of Taiwan after their defeat by the communists.

blocks.text: For decades, two governments have vied for the title of China's sole legitimate representative. The shift occurred in 1971, when the UN withdrew its headquarters from Taipei to give it to Beijing. Taiwan finds itself diplomatically isolated, while retaining its currency, its army and an elected government.
The Kuomintang took so much art when it fled the mainland in 1949 that the National Palace Museum in Taipei now has one of the richest collections of Chinese art in the world.

sections.title: The silicon shield: TSMC and the global challenge

blocks.text: Diplomatically isolated, Taiwan is undergoing a spectacular economic metamorphosis. The island specializes in high technology, giving birth in 1987 to **[[TSMC (Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company)]]**, which has become the heart of the global semiconductor industry, with more than 90% of the most advanced chips.

blocks.caption: TSMC manufactures the vast majority of the world's most advanced electronic chips in Taiwan.

blocks.text: This supremacy creates a “silicon shield”. The entire world is so dependent on Taiwanese factories that an invasion would cripple global production chains, from artificial intelligence to automobiles.

This success is accompanied by a major political transition. After decades of authoritarian rule, Taiwan is becoming one of Asia's most liberal democracies. In 1996, its first elections to **direct universal suffrage** marked a break with the Chinese model.

Taiwan's survival depends on a subtle diplomatic game orchestrated by Washington. Since a 1979 law, the United States has practiced **[[American strategic ambiguity]]**: they officially recognize Beijing, but provide Taiwan with the means of its defense, without ever clearly saying whether they would intervene militarily in the event of an attack.

This fragile balance pursues two goals: to dissuade Beijing from attacking for fear of an American response, and to dissuade Taipei from declaring official independence which would trigger war. But this balance is increasingly being tested by repeated incursions by Chinese military aircraft into the island's air defense zone, the **ZIDA**.

blocks.caption: Incursions by Chinese military aircraft into Taiwanese airspace have increased in recent years.

blocks.text: Xi Jinping's speeches, affirming that the Taiwan question cannot be passed on indefinitely to subsequent generations, worry observers. The United States is gradually clarifying its support, which increases the risk of a direct confrontation between the two superpowers.

The conflict is no longer limited to missiles: it extends to cyberspace and disinformation. Taiwan suffers millions of cyberattacks every day intended to destabilize its democracy. The issue is also symbolic: Taiwan proves that a Chinese world can prosper under a democratic regime.

The situation is complicated by economic interdependence: China remains the island's largest trading partner, which slows escalation. Among the younger generation, the feeling of belonging to a distinct nation is growing, while Beijing has toughened its diplomacy since the forced integration of Hong Kong.
In 2021, after a Chinese embargo on its products, Taiwan launched the “freedom pineapples” campaign: massive consumption of local pineapples which transformed the fruit into a symbol of resistance.
Taiwan is the greatest current geopolitical paradox: a territory not recognized by the UN, but which has become indispensable to the technological and economic survival of all the great world powers.
